name: Caffeine
lethalBasis: human estimate (about 150-200 mg/kg reported)
notes: The FDA puts toxic effects (racing heart, dangerous heart rhythms, seizures) at roughly 1.2 g, and life-threatening doses typically at 10 to 14 g, though less can be dangerous for children and sensitive people. Pure caffeine powder is far more dangerous than drinks: one teaspoon equals roughly 28 cups of coffee, and it is almost impossible to measure safely at home.

name: Table salt (sodium chloride)
lethalBasis: low end of the reported human range (0.5-1 g/kg)
notes: The daily guidance of 2,300 mg is for sodium, which equals about 5.75 g of salt (a bit under one teaspoon). Salt poisoning is a real risk, especially in small children. Never use salt water to induce vomiting. No firm threshold for toxic effects is shown because published figures vary too widely.

toxicNote: No reliable human dose threshold. Early signs are strong thirst, weakness and nausea; severe cases bring confusion, muscle twitching and seizures.

name: Alcohol (ethanol)
notes: About 0.8 g of pure ethanol per kg (roughly 3 to 4 drinks) brings a blood alcohol level of about 0.10. Drinking fast can be dangerous at far lower amounts, and children are much more vulnerable. US guidance is up to 1 drink a day for women and 2 for men. Blood alcohol is estimated from your body water (Hume and Weyers equations) and a 0.84 blood water factor, so real values vary. Signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, vomiting, slow or irregular breathing, passing out. Call 911.

NIAAA: Alcohol poisoning

lethalNote: No single fatal dose can be given, because tolerance varies enormously. A clinical reference says severe intoxication can develop at about 1 to 1.5 mL of pure ethanol per kg (roughly 0.8 to 1.2 g/kg), and death is usually linked to blood levels above about 80 to 90 mmol/L (roughly 0.37 to 0.41 percent), though it can be higher in regular heavy drinkers. Children can be harmed by very small amounts. Call 911.

name: Nutmeg
notes: Normal cooking amounts are fine. Poisoning has been reported at about 5 g (roughly 2 teaspoons): nausea, racing heart, confusion, hallucinations, lasting a day or longer. Fatalities are very rare and no lethal dose is established.

safeNote: No official daily limit. Normal cooking amounts are not a concern.
lethalNote: No established fatal dose. Deaths are very rare.

name: Sugar (sucrose)
lethalBasis: rat LD50; not a realistic human figure
notes: The lethal figure comes from rats. A person could not realistically eat that much, and the real harms of sugar are long-term, not a single-dose poisoning. The guidance limit is the American Heart Association figure for added sugar for most women and children over 2 (36 g for most men).

toxicNote: Not acutely toxic to people at realistic amounts. Rats given huge doses showed sluggishness and diarrhea. The harm from sugar is long-term, not from a single dose.

name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol, paracetamol)
notes: The Extra Strength label limit is 6 tablets (3,000 mg) in 24 hours; other products have different limits, so check your label. Accidental overdose is common because acetaminophen is hidden in many cold, flu and sleep products. Count every source. An overdose can feel fine for the first day while liver damage develops, so call Poison Control immediately if more than directed was taken.

safeNote: This app does not give a safe daily amount for nicotine from tobacco or vapes. For quit-smoking products, follow the label (see Nicotine gum).
toxicNote: In reported cases, swallowing tobacco or nicotine gum at doses up to about 6 mg per kg caused poisoning symptoms without death. A smaller body gets a bigger dose per kg, so a swallow an adult might shrug off can poison a child.
lethalNote: The widely repeated adult fatal dose of 30 to 60 mg (about 0.5 to 1 mg per kg) traces back to dubious 19th-century self-experiments. A 2014 review in Archives of Toxicology estimates an oral LD50 of about 6.5 to 13 mg per kg instead, and notes people have survived far larger amounts. That is one toxicologist's estimate and is still debated, so do not treat it as a safe margin: any swallow, especially of concentrated e-liquid or by a child, is an emergency.
name: Nicotine
servingName: nicotine absorbed from one cigarette (about 2 mg)
notes: Smoking one cigarette takes up about 2 mg of nicotine, according to the same review. Check the label for the nicotine amount in any product. Call Poison Control right away for any swallow.

There is no simple antidote; treatment is intensive supportive care and sometimes a liver transplant. No fatal dose is established; toxicity depends on the plant part, season and the person.

notes: Do not wait for symptoms. Seek help immediately and keep a piece of the mushroom for identification. Look-alikes make wild mushrooms impossible to judge unless you are an expert, and the Western destroying angel is also dangerous. safeNote: Do not swallow, and never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or toilet bowl cleaners.
toxicNote: Typical household bleach is 4 to 8 percent sodium hypochlorite. One or two mouthfuls usually cause minor mouth and throat irritation, stomach upset and vomiting. Larger amounts or stronger types, such as pool bleach, cause worse symptoms.
lethalNote: Concentrated bleach can cause permanent damage to the stomach and gut and may result in death. No fatal dose is established.
name: Bleach
notes: Mixing bleach with ammonia makes chlorine gas, which can cause choking and serious breathing problems. If swallowed, follow Poison Control's directions; MedlinePlus says to give water or milk right away unless a provider says not to. Call 1-800-222-1222 for any swallow, eye splash or breathing trouble. Poison centers advise never storing bleach in a cup or food container.

safeNote: Not for eating. Keep pods out of sight and reach of children.
toxicNote: Biting into a pod can cause coughing, choking, trouble breathing and coma. The detergent can also irritate the skin and burn the eyes. Pods cause more stomach irritation and more breathing problems and drowsiness than liquid detergent.
lethalNote: Poison Control lists severe vomiting, severe breathing trouble, esophagus burns and coma as possible effects. No fatal dose is established.

notes: Laundry packets are more concentrated than regular detergent. Store them in the closed original container, up high or locked. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away for any swallow or exposure.

safeNote: Never swallow. Keep batteries and any device with a loose battery away from children.
toxicNote: When a battery is swallowed it is impossible to know whether it will pass or get stuck. A coin-shaped battery caught in the esophagus can cause serious burns in as little as two hours, and larger button batteries can burn a hole through the esophagus or cause death.
lethalNote: This is an emergency, not a dose question. Do not wait for symptoms to appear.
name: Button batteries
notes: If anyone swallows a battery of any size, call the National Battery Ingestion Hotline at 1-800-498-8666 (24 hours) or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 immediately, and go to the emergency room. Over 3,500 people a year in the US swallow button batteries. Watch for coughing, drooling, trouble swallowing, refusing to eat or drink, and fever. Tape over discarded button batteries before throwing them away.

notes: MedlinePlus warns metformin may rarely cause a serious, life-threatening condition called lactic acidosis. Risk is higher with kidney disease, age over 65, certain heart or liver conditions, heavy alcohol use and some other medicines. safeNote: EFSA says eating more than three small raw apricot kernels (about 370 mg) in one serving can exceed the safe level for adults. For a toddler, even one small kernel can exceed it. EFSA's safe one-off level for cyanide is 20 micrograms per kg of body weight.
toxicNote: Chewing or grinding raw apricot kernels turns amygdalin into cyanide. Cyanide poisoning can cause nausea, fever, headache, insomnia, thirst, lethargy, nervousness, aches and pains, and falling blood pressure.
lethalNote: In extreme cases cyanide poisoning is fatal. EFSA reports a lethal cyanide dose of 0.5 to 3.5 mg per kg of body weight. Kernels vary a lot in how much amygdalin they hold, so there is no safe count to rely on.
name: Apricot kernels
notes: EFSA says the apricot fruit itself is not a concern, only the kernel inside the stone. EFSA's assessment was prompted by sellers promoting 10 to 60 kernels a day as a cancer remedy; EFSA says judging cancer claims was outside its remit, and its finding is that those intakes are unsafe. If someone ate kernels and feels unwell, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

sources.title: EFSA: Apricot kernels pose risk of cyanide poisoning

safeNote: FDA advice: no matter your age, don't eat large amounts of black licorice at one time. The warning does not apply to red licorice, which has little or no licorice root.
toxicNote: The FDA says if you are 40 or older, eating 2 ounces of black licorice a day for at least two weeks could land you in the hospital with an irregular heart rhythm. The cause is glycyrrhizin, which can lower potassium and also cause high blood pressure, swelling, lethargy and congestive heart failure.
lethalNote: A New England Journal of Medicine case report describes a 54-year-old man who died of cardiac arrest after eating about a bag and a half of black licorice daily for a few weeks, as reported by ABC News. No fatal dose is established.
name: Black licorice
notes: Potassium levels usually return to normal with no permanent problems once you stop. Licorice can also interact with some medicines and supplements, so ask a health professional. If you have eaten a lot and have an irregular heartbeat or muscle weakness, stop eating it and contact your health care provider.

sources.title: American Heart Association News: Black licorice is a candy that should inspire caution

safeNote: Never eat raw or undercooked red kidney beans. Boil dried beans properly before eating or adding to dishes.
toxicNote: The FDA Bad Bug Book says as few as four or five raw beans can trigger symptoms. Illness usually begins 1 to 3 hours after eating, with extreme nausea, then vomiting that may be very severe, followed by diarrhea.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established. People normally feel better within a few hours, though some cases needed hospital care.
name: Raw kidney beans
notes: Raw red kidney beans carry 20,000 to 70,000 hemagglutinating units of the toxin phytohaemagglutinin, against 200 to 400 once fully cooked. The FDA Bad Bug Book says heating to 80 degrees C can make beans about five times more toxic than raw, and slow cookers often do not get hot enough, so beans should be boiled first. White kidney beans carry about a third as much toxin as red.

safeNote: MedlinePlus says potatoes that are not green and have had any sprouts removed are safe to eat. Never eat potatoes that are spoiled or green below the skin, and always throw away sprouts.
toxicNote: The poison is solanine, which MedlinePlus calls very toxic even in small amounts. Effects are mostly stomach and gut problems, often delayed 8 to 10 hours; nervous system effects can occur with large amounts. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, headache, hallucinations, delirium, dilated pupils and vision changes.
lethalNote: MedlinePlus says these poisonings can be very dangerous, and severe cases can bring paralysis, slow breathing, slow pulse and shock. No fatal dose is established.
name: Green potato
notes: The Tokyo Metropolitan Government notes solanine is almost not broken down by cooking, baking or other heating, so remove green parts and sprouts completely. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

safeNote: Eat only the stalks. MedlinePlus says the poison is in the leaf blade, while the stalk can be eaten.
toxicNote: MedlinePlus lists oxalic acid, and possibly anthraquinone glycosides, as the poisonous ingredients. Symptoms include burning and blisters in the mouth and throat, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, kidney stones, red-colored urine, seizures and coma.
lethalNote: Deaths have been reported but are rare, according to an older MedlinePlus version. No fatal dose is established.

safeNote: Do not give honey to a baby under 12 months old, in any form, including on a pacifier or baked into food. It is the only known way to prevent infant botulism from honey.
toxicNote: Honey can carry Clostridium botulinum spores. In babies under a year the spores can grow in the gut and make toxin, causing infant botulism. A survey cited by the University of Florida found spores in 10 percent of US honey samples.
lethalNote: Infant botulism is a serious illness. This app does not give a fatal amount for honey.
name: Honey
notes: The CDC, American Academy of Pediatrics and National Honey Board recommend no honey for infants under 12 months, according to University of Florida extension. After age one the digestive system is more mature and illness from spores is much less likely. If you think a baby has symptoms, get medical care at once.

safeNote: FDA and EPA advise people who might become pregnant, are pregnant or breastfeeding, and children to avoid king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, shark, swordfish, Gulf of Mexico tilefish and bigeye tuna. These have the highest mercury levels.
toxicNote: Mercury in fish can be harmful to the brain and nervous system if a person is exposed to too much over time, according to EPA. This is a long-term exposure risk, not a single-meal dose.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established for mercury from fish.
name: High-mercury fish (shark, swordfish, king mackerel)
notes: FDA and EPA advise 2 to 3 servings a week from the Best Choices list, or 1 serving from the Good Choices list. An adult serving is 4 ounces, about the palm of your hand. For children a serving is about 1 ounce at age 1 to 3, 2 ounces at 4 to 7, 3 ounces at 8 to 10 and 4 ounces at 11. Canned and fresh albacore (white) tuna and yellowfin tuna are Good Choices.

servingName: 12 oz can or bottle at about 5% alcohol (1 standard drink)
name: Beer
notes: Every figure is for pure alcohol, not the whole drink. One US standard drink holds 14 g of pure alcohol, and this amount comes from the serving named here at the typical strength. Many beers, wines, and drinks are stronger and count as more than one drink, so check the label. Never use these numbers to decide whether it is safe to drive. The 2020-2025 Dietary Guidelines say 2 drinks or less a day for men and 1 or less for women, and that adults can also choose not to drink. The newer 2025-2030 guidelines no longer give a number. Signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, vomiting, slow or irregular breathing, passing out. Call 911.

lethalNote: No single fatal dose can be given, because tolerance varies enormously. A clinical reference says severe intoxication can develop at about 1 to 1.5 mL of pure ethanol per kg (roughly 0.8 to 1.2 g/kg), and death is usually linked to blood levels above about 80 to 90 mmol/L (roughly 0.37 to 0.41 percent), though it can be higher in regular heavy drinkers. Children can be harmed by very small amounts. Call 911.
